contraindications: Uncertain; not specified in the text
original_extraction.evidence_text:
Pleasant feelings such as satisfaction, joy and love are natural byproducts of living by your values.
But they aren’t the only ones. Other byproducts include uncomfortable emotions such as fear,
sadness, anger, frustration and disappointment. You can’t have just the pleasant feelings without all
the others. That’s why it’s important to learn how to accept all your feelings—pleasant, neutral and
unpleasant.

---

Q: Lots of self-help approaches suggest that when we are feeling bad we should try things like
having a hot bath, listening to music, reading a good book, savouring a hot chocolate, getting a
massage, walking the dog, playing a sport we love, spending time with friends, and so on. Are you
suggesting we shouldn’t try such activities?

---

A: This is similar to a question I answered in Chapter 2. I’m sure you’ve had plenty of great advice
from all sorts of sources about helpful activities to try when you’re feeling ‘bad’. And most of
these activities can be deeply satisfying—as long as you genuinely value them; that is, as long as
you engage in them out of a sense that they are truly meaningful to you. But if you do these
activities mainly to run away from unpleasant feelings, they aren’t likely to be all that rewarding—
it’s hard to appreciate life when you’re on the run from something threatening.

---

Therefore, in ACT, acceptance always comes first. First you make room for your feelings and
allow them to be exactly as they are. Then you ask, ‘What can I do right now that is truly
meaningful or important?” This is very different from asking, * How canI feel better?” Then, once
you’ve identified an activity you truly value, go ahead and take action.

---

You can remember these three steps with a simple acronym:
generation_rules: First accept feelings as they are
Then ask what is truly meaningful or important to do now
Finally, take action on the identified valued activity
pause_rules: Pause after acceptance step to allow emotional space before moving to action planning
original_extraction.psychological_function: Encourages emotional acceptance, reduces experiential avoidance, and enhances value-driven behavior.
repetition_rules: Repeat the three-step process (acceptance, identify values, act) to reinforce learning
symbolic_elements: Acronym representing three steps: acceptance, identifying meaningful action, taking action
original_extraction.therapeutic_function: Facilitates acceptance of all emotions (pleasant, neutral, unpleasant) and promotes engagement in meaningful activities aligned with personal values.
voice_rules: Use a guiding and validating tone emphasizing acceptance before action
Distinguish between acting to avoid feelings and acting from values
